newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma economy growing, but problems remain-ADB.
newsitem.headline: Burma economy growing, but problems remain-ADB.

text.p: Burma's economy is continuing to grow but structural problems, high inflation and poverty are problems that must still be addressed by the military government, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said on Thursday.

"The economy of Myanmar (Burma) again performed quite well in 1996," the Manila-based ADB said in its annual report. "However, to facilitate the economy's transition to a higher growth path, the government has to address several structural problems."
It said although the government had introduced some market-oriented economic reforms it has yet to implement measures to ensure greater openness and competitiveness.
The ADB report said Burma needed to address infrastructure bottlenecks in transport, shipping, ports and utilities.

Burma's real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by about six percent in fiscal 1996/97, the ADB said, compared to 7.7 percent in the previous fiscal year. The 1996/97 fiscal year ended on March 31, 1997.
The ADB said if the economic reform process continues and helps improve the trade and fiscal imbalances, Burma could see GDP growth of about 6.0-6.5 percent in 1997 and 1998.

The agriculture sector, which accounts for 38 percent of the nation's output and 67 percent of employment, grew by 5.4 percent in 1996. Finance was the fastest-growing sector, with an increase of 14.6 percent over the previous year while mining grew by over 13 percent and manufacturing by 10 percent.
The report said Burma was affected by a slump in garment exports in 1996 due in part to the decision of some leading U.S. manufacturers to stop sourcing their products from Burma.

Several major American apparel companies like Oshkosh B'Gosh Inc, Liz Clairborne and Spiegel unit Eddie Bauer have pulled out of Burma amid consumer protests about the government's human rights record.

"The budget deficit was reduced as a result of strict control over government expenses," the ADB report said. "However, deep cuts in non-military public expenditures had adverse distributional impacts."
The report did not give any figures for the deficit. But it said defence accounted for 45 percent of the budget, and at the same time spending on health and education declined.

"Inflation remained excessive," the report said. "While official figures for April 1996 indicated inflation at 22.5 percent on a year-on-year basis, other sources suggested it could be as high as 30-40 percent."
The ADB report said poverty remained a fundamental challenge in Burma, with an estimated 40 percent of the population living below the poverty line.
